overview: The German Empire, founded in 1871 under Prussian leadership, joined many German states in a constitutional monarchy. Its factories, laboratories and cities grew quickly, but so did demands for fair wages, political voice and decent housing. Its government also ruled African colonies and committed mass violence against Herero and Nama people. The First World War brought catastrophic loss, shortages and revolution. The imperial monarchy ended in November 1918, two years before the imported map interval closes.

periods.title: Unification and a new imperial government
periods.summary: Following the Franco-Prussian War, German states formed an empire led by the Prussian king as emperor. A constitution created federal institutions and an elected Reichstag, while the monarch and appointed chancellor kept powerful roles.

periods.title: Industry and worker insurance
periods.summary: Growing factories and crowded cities brought labor demands. Laws in 1883, 1884 and 1889 created health, accident and old-age/disability insurance for many workers, although protection remained limited and contested.

periods.title: Big cities, science and social movements
periods.summary: Urban housing, transport and sanitation changed unevenly. Women organized for education and public life; researchers investigated infectious disease. Berlin's experience cannot stand for every rural region.

periods.title: Colonial violence and reform campaigns
periods.summary: German colonial forces committed genocide against Herero and Nama communities in what is now Namibia. At home, movements argued over housing, social reform and political rights; women gained wider association rights in 1908.

periods.title: World war and imperial collapse
periods.summary: War brought mass death, rationing and hunger to soldiers and families. Sailors' revolt spread into the November 1918 revolution; the monarchy ended and a republic was proclaimed on 9 November.

periods.title: Life after the emperor
periods.summary: The German Empire's monarchy ended, but its people and places did not. A republican government followed amid postwar hardship; the map's 1914-1920 polygon should not be read as two extra years of imperial rule.

items.text: In January 1871 German rulers proclaimed a new empire during war with France. The Prussian king became German emperor. The new state joined existing kingdoms and principalities; it did not invent all their people or institutions in a single ceremony.

The 1871 constitution gave the empire an elected Reichstag alongside a Bundesrat of state representatives. The emperor appointed the chancellor and commanded the military. Voting for one chamber did not give voters full control over the government.

The empire took colonies overseas. In German South West Africa, now Namibia, Herero and Nama people resisted settler rule. German forces killed many, deliberately drove people toward thirst and hunger, imprisoned survivors and seized land. The Federal Archives calls the Herero campaign genocide.

Industrial growth drew families to cities. A 1903 Berlin survey counted hundreds of thousands of one- and two-room apartments, while wealthy families occupied grand homes. One city could contain very different ideas of what “home” meant.

Many working women earned money because a household could not live on one wage. The work might be in a factory, shop or home; income and duties differed by class and place. Family life was shaped by wages as much as by official speeches.

Women's associations campaigned for access to education and jobs. An umbrella federation formed in 1894, and women could join political parties after a 1908 law. Women still lacked a Reichstag vote during the imperial monarchy.

Schools did not all teach the same subjects. Traditional Gymnasien emphasized classical languages, while Realschulen and Realgymnasien offered more modern languages and sciences. In Prussia, women gained regular university enrollment in the 1908-09 winter term, later than many men.
Berlin streets gained gas, electric light and new transport, but such changes did not spread to every household at once. A city newcomer might ride a tram to work and still return to a crowded room.
Berlin's first electric street tram ran in 1881, while household electric connections remained uncommon even in 1914. For a child, a humming tram and a dark home could belong to the same city.

Around 1900, reform groups argued for better housing, hygiene, child-centered education and even environmental protection. Women and men built associations to press these causes; not every reformer agreed on politics, but social change was not only an order from above.

The Kaiser Wilhelm Society for research was founded in Berlin in 1911. Laboratories and universities could pursue new science, while school routes still differed by class and sex. The prestige of research did not erase unequal access to learning.

sections.title: Medicine, drains and the necessary stop

items.text: In Berlin in 1882, Robert Koch announced identification of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. It was a major step in understanding infection, not an instant cure for every sick person.

Worker laws began health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and disability insurance in 1889. These protections grew from political pressure and government goals, but did not cover everyone or silence workers who wanted stronger rights.

Berlin commissioned a sewerage expansion in 1873 because wastewater running through streets threatened health. A drain beneath a street was an engineering achievement, but its benefits depended on connections, maintenance and where a family lived.

Berlin had two public urinals by 1863. Decorative iron “Café Achteck” urinals were planned from 1878, but public toilets for both women and men appeared around 1900. Even the capital needed time to decide that everyone might need a stop.

The 1871 imperial constitution law opens “Wir Wilhelm, von Gottes Gnaden Deutscher Kaiser”. In English, that means “We Wilhelm, by the grace of God German Emperor.” It is a short sample of written German from a published transcription of a period law, reflecting the ruler's official voice.
A law's royal first line is not proof everyone in the empire spoke exactly like the court. Regional dialects, other languages and social experiences were more varied than this ceremonial sentence.

Jewish people had gained civic equality in law, but an antisemitic petition campaigned to cut back those rights. Legal wording and public prejudice could move in opposite directions. The petition shows the harm of organized exclusion, not the views of every German resident.

Food cards did not supply enough for many families during the First World War. The 1916-17 “turnip winter” became a memory of hunger; women carried household and paid-work burdens while relatives served at the front. These were unequal hardships, not a quaint menu change.

In November 1918, revolt among sailors spread to Berlin. The emperor's abdication was announced and Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic on 9 November. The monarchy ended; German communities did not vanish with a change of government.

ending.text: Defeat in the First World War and a widening revolution ended the German Empire's monarchy in November 1918. A republic was proclaimed on 9 November, while German people, families and institutions continued through a difficult transition. The imported 1914 to 1920 map interval extends beyond this political ending; it does not verify borders or prolong the emperor's reign.

sources.title: Robert Koch Institute, Robert Koch
sources.note: Koch announced tuberculosis pathogen discovery in Berlin 24 March 1882; medical advance did not instantly cure patients.

sources.note: Berlin commissioned Hobrecht sewerage expansion in 1873 against dangerous street wastewater; capital-specific infrastructure.
